\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

When language models train iteratively on their own output, the training distribution progressively loses its tail modes, a phenomenon termed model collapse~\cite{shumailov2024curse,alemohammad2024mad}.
Lexical diversity narrows, calibration deteriorates, and each generation inherits the systematic biases of its predecessors.
As machine-generated text becomes prevalent on the web, such feedback loops pose a growing and often invisible risk to production training pipelines.
By the time standard quality metrics register degradation, the underlying distribution may have already shifted irreversibly.
This threat motivates the search for cheap-to-compute \emph{canary metrics}: leading indicators that signal distributional degradation before expensive downstream measures reveal the full extent of collapse.
The concept parallels early-warning signals for critical transitions in ecological systems~\cite{scheffer2009early,scheffer2012anticipating}, where proxy indicators allow intervention before a tipping point.

Yet a fundamental question remains unanswered: \emph{at what contamination level does Granger-causal detection of collapse become possible?}
Whether a candidate canary genuinely \emph{precedes} downstream degradation or merely correlates with it under shared non-stationary trends depends on contamination regime and statistical method in ways that existing analyses leave unresolved.
Iterative training produces short, noisy time series (often fewer than 15 points per generation sequence), where detection power drops sharply and false positive rates can be high~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.

We identify four methodological gaps in existing lead-lag analyses of iterative collapse.
(1)~No differencing tests rule out spurious regression from shared non-stationary trends~\cite{granger1974spurious}.
(2)~Conclusions rest on a single statistical method whose assumptions about stationarity and directionality are rarely examined.
(3)~No FDR correction guards against spurious findings when testing many metric pairs simultaneously.
(4)~No regime-dependent analysis is performed, despite the possibility that the same test yields opposite conclusions at different contamination levels.

We discover a \emph{detection phase transition} in canary-based monitoring of iterative collapse---a steep onset of statistical detectability at a critical mixing ratio; this is a detection-theoretic boundary, not a thermodynamic phase transition.
Using Pythia-410M~\cite{biderman2023pythia} across thirteen contamination levels ($\alpha \in [0, 1]$, thirteen values from 0.00 to 1.00) and up to four random seeds, we show that Granger-causal detectability undergoes a steep onset at per-generation mixing ratio $\alpha_c{=}0.476$ at $T{=}10$ generations (sigmoid $R^2{=}0.969$, $\Delta\alpha{\approx}0.02$): permutation Granger causality (PermG) jumps from 0/8 FDR-significant metric pairs at $\alpha{\leq}0.45$ to 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$.
A signal-times-resolution ($S \times R$) framework explains this onset and the non-monotonic dose-response through competing signal strength and temporal resolution.
A multi-method consensus framework (MMCT) comparing five statistical methods reveals that method choice alone can shift conclusions on the same data from universal significance to complete null.
Cross-architecture validation across 15 model-seed combinations spanning six families (345M--6.9B) confirms PermG detection (${\geq}6/8$) in 13 cases (87\%).
Granger precedence in our framework establishes temporal predictive improvement, not true causality~\cite{shojaie2022granger}; our canary claim is scoped to diversity metrics (distinct-$n$~\cite{li2016diversity}), not model collapse broadly.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Detection phase transition} (\S\ref{sec:regime}).
    At $T{=}10$, PermG jumps from 0/8 FDR-significant pairs through $\alpha{=}0.45$ to 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$ ($\alpha_c{=}0.476$, sigmoid $R^2{=}0.969$, $\Delta\alpha{\approx}0.02$), with a four-regime structure: \emph{blind}, \emph{onset}, \emph{synchronous dip}, and \emph{detection}.
    At $\alpha{=}0.10$, a canary blind spot emerges: diversity has already collapsed but canary metrics remain indistinguishable from the null.
    Cross-architecture validation across 15 model-seed combinations confirms detection in 13 cases (87\%).

    \item \textbf{Signal-times-resolution interpretive framework} (\S\ref{sec:theory}).
    A power interpretation formalizes the onset as $\mathrm{Power}(\alpha, T) = \Phi(S \cdot R \cdot \sqrt{T}/\sigma)$, generating three testable predictions for $T{=}20$; sub-threshold PermG $p$-values at $\alpha{=}0.45$ ($p{=}0.059$--$0.091$) are consistent with proximity to the power boundary.

    \item \textbf{Multi-method diagnostic toolkit} (\S\ref{sec:method}).
    The MMCT exposes three pitfalls: naive cross-correlation has 75\% null-control FPR ($\kappa{=}0.185$ inter-method), first-differencing eliminates canary$\to$perplexity associations entirely while preserving all canary$\to$diversity leads (24/24$\to$24/24), and regime dependence causes the same test to shift from 5--6/8 FDR-significant pairs per seed at $\alpha{\geq}0.75$ to 0/8 at $\alpha{\leq}0.45$.
    PermG identifies token entropy as a one-generation-ahead canary for diversity collapse (24/24 forward, 0/24 reverse).

    \item \textbf{Canary-based early detection} (\S\ref{sec:intervention}).
    We demonstrate that canary signals can be operationalized: a proof-of-concept predictive cessation protocol reduces peak perplexity by 58\% (bootstrap 95\% CI: 29--64\%) and fires one generation earlier than reactive cessation.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Dose-Response and the $S \times R$ Framework}
\label{sec:dose_response}

The PermG dose-response profile (Figure~\ref{fig:regime_map}) reveals four detection regimes: \emph{blind} ($\alpha \leq 0.45$, 0/8 FDR-significant pairs), \emph{onset} ($\alpha \approx 0.50$, 6/8), \emph{synchronous dip} ($\alpha \approx 0.60$, 0/8 both seeds; dual-seed confirmed), and \emph{detection} ($\alpha \geq 0.75$, 5--6/8 per seed across 3~seeds; $\alpha{=}1.0$, 6/8 across 4~seeds).
The non-monotonic dip at $\alpha{=}0.60$ is consistent with the $S \times R$ framework (\S\ref{sec:theory}): signal strength $S(\alpha)$ rises monotonically with contamination, but temporal resolution $R(\alpha)$ drops when relaxation time approaches the observation interval.
At $\alpha \approx 0.60$, this compression drives the canary-to-downstream lag toward zero, and the product $S \times R$ reaches a local minimum.
The synchronous zone is mechanistically distinct from the blind spot: in the blind zone, canary drift is indistinguishable from the null; in the synchronous zone, both canary and downstream metrics drift substantially but without temporal offset.

Method choice is itself a major source of analytic variability.
At $\alpha{=}1.0$, direction-checked forward significance rates span 0\% to 75\%: naive and differenced cross-correlation fall to 0/8 after lag-direction filtering (all significant correlations peak at negative lags), while PermG achieves 6/8 (Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison}). Inter-method agreement is $\kappa{=}0.185$ (near chance).
PermG is the only method that combines zero null-control FPR with consistent detection at $\alpha \geq 0.50$ (Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison}); its nonparametric null distribution, built-in directionality, and hyperparameter-free design explain this advantage.
The $S \times R$ framework generates three testable predictions for $T{=}20$ via $\mathrm{Power}(\alpha, T) = \Phi(S \cdot R \cdot \sqrt{T}/\sigma)$: (i)~$\alpha_c$ at $T{=}10$ should left-shift, (ii)~the transition should smooth, and (iii)~different methods should exhibit different $\alpha_c$ values.
These predictions are under empirical verification.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

When language models train iteratively on their own output, the training distribution progressively loses its tail modes, a phenomenon termed model collapse~\cite{shumailov2024curse,alemohammad2024mad}.
Lexical diversity narrows, calibration deteriorates, and each generation inherits the systematic biases of its predecessors.
As machine-generated text becomes prevalent on the web, such feedback loops pose a growing and often invisible risk to production training pipelines.
By the time standard quality metrics register degradation, the underlying distribution may have already shifted irreversibly.
This threat motivates the search for cheap-to-compute \emph{canary metrics}: leading indicators that signal distributional degradation before expensive downstream measures reveal the full extent of collapse.
The concept parallels early-warning signals for critical transitions in ecological systems~\cite{scheffer2009early,scheffer2012anticipating}, where proxy indicators allow intervention before a tipping point.

Yet a fundamental question remains unanswered: \emph{at what contamination level does Granger-causal detection of collapse become possible?}
Whether a candidate canary genuinely \emph{precedes} downstream degradation or merely correlates with it under shared non-stationary trends depends on contamination regime and statistical method in ways that existing analyses leave unresolved.
Iterative training produces short, noisy time series (often fewer than 15 points per generation sequence), where detection power drops sharply and false positive rates can be high~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.

We identify four methodological gaps in existing lead-lag analyses of iterative collapse.
(1)~No differencing tests rule out spurious regression from shared non-stationary trends~\cite{granger1974spurious}.
(2)~Conclusions rest on a single statistical method whose assumptions about stationarity and directionality are rarely examined.
(3)~No FDR correction guards against spurious findings when testing many metric pairs simultaneously.
(4)~No regime-dependent analysis is performed, despite the possibility that the same test yields opposite conclusions at different contamination levels.

We discover a \emph{detection phase transition} in canary-based monitoring of iterative collapse---a steep onset of statistical detectability at a critical mixing ratio; this is a detection-theoretic boundary, not a thermodynamic phase transition.
Using Pythia-410M~\cite{biderman2023pythia} across thirteen contamination levels ($\alpha \in [0, 1]$, thirteen values from 0.00 to 1.00) and up to four random seeds, we show that Granger-causal detectability undergoes a steep onset at per-generation mixing ratio $\alpha_c{=}0.476$ at $T{=}10$ generations (sigmoid $R^2{=}0.969$, $\Delta\alpha{\approx}0.02$): permutation Granger causality (PermG) jumps from 0/8 FDR-significant metric pairs at $\alpha{\leq}0.45$ to 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$.
A signal-times-resolution ($S \times R$) framework explains this onset and the non-monotonic dose-response through competing signal strength and temporal resolution.
A multi-method consensus framework (MMCT) comparing five statistical methods reveals that method choice alone can shift conclusions on the same data from universal significance to complete null.
Cross-architecture validation across 15 model-seed combinations spanning six families (345M--6.9B) confirms PermG detection (${\geq}6/8$) in 13 cases (87\%).
Granger precedence in our framework establishes temporal predictive improvement, not true causality~\cite{shojaie2022granger}; our canary claim is scoped to diversity metrics (distinct-$n$~\cite{li2016diversity}), not model collapse broadly.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Detection phase transition} (\S\ref{sec:regime}).
    At $T{=}10$, PermG jumps from 0/8 FDR-significant pairs through $\alpha{=}0.45$ to 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$ ($\alpha_c{=}0.476$, sigmoid $R^2{=}0.969$, $\Delta\alpha{\approx}0.02$), with a four-regime structure: \emph{blind}, \emph{onset}, \emph{synchronous dip}, and \emph{detection}.
    At $\alpha{=}0.10$, a canary blind spot emerges: diversity has already collapsed but canary metrics remain indistinguishable from the null.
    Cross-architecture validation across 15 model-seed combinations confirms detection in 13 cases (87\%).

    \item \textbf{Multi-method diagnostic toolkit} (\S\ref{sec:method}).
    The MMCT exposes three pitfalls: naive cross-correlation has 75\% null-control FPR ($\kappa{=}0.185$ inter-method), first-differencing eliminates canary$\to$perplexity associations entirely while preserving all canary$\to$diversity leads (24/24$\to$24/24), and regime dependence causes the same test to shift from 5--6/8 FDR-significant pairs per seed at $\alpha{\geq}0.75$ to 0/8 at $\alpha{\leq}0.45$.
    PermG identifies token entropy as a one-generation-ahead canary for diversity collapse (24/24 forward, 0/24 reverse).

    \item \textbf{Canary-based early detection} (\S\ref{sec:intervention}).
    We demonstrate that canary signals can be operationalized: a proof-of-concept predictive cessation protocol reduces peak perplexity by 58\% (bootstrap 95\% CI: 29--64\%) and fires one generation earlier than reactive cessation.
\end{enumerate}

The steep onset at $\alpha_c{=}0.476$ is detailed in \S\ref{sec:dose_response}.}
\label{fig:regime_map}
\end{figure*}

2	\label{sec:method}
3	
4	\paragraph{Methodological pitfalls.}
5	\label{sec:pitfalls}
6	Lead-lag analysis in iterative model collapse is fragile along three axes, each documented with data from \S\ref{sec:regime}--\ref{sec:dose_response}.
7	\emph{Method sensitivity}: five detection methods applied to identical data ($\alpha{=}1.0$, 8 validated canary$\to$downstream pairs, direction-checked) yield forward significance rates spanning 0\% to 75\%, with inter-method agreement at $\kappa{=}0.185$ and naive cross-correlation reaching 75\% null-control FPR.
8	\emph{Spurious regression}: first-differencing to remove shared trends~\cite{granger1974spurious} eliminates canary$\to$perplexity associations ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$) while preserving canary$\to$diversity (24/24$\to$24/24), exposing an entire analysis channel as trend-driven rather than temporally precedent.
9	\emph{Regime dependence}: the same Granger test finds 0/8 pairs significant through $\alpha{=}0.45$ but 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$, a categorical shift at a 5-percentage-point boundary that a single-$\alpha$ study would miss entirely.
10	These pitfalls motivate systematic method comparison rather than reliance on any single detection approach.
11	
12	\paragraph{Multi-Method Consensus Test (MMCT).}
13	\label{sec:mmct}
14	We apply the Multi-Method Consensus Test, a weighted consensus framework in the specification curve~\cite{simonsohn2020specification} and multi-method early-warning~\cite{scheffer2009early,bell2022modeling} traditions, adapted to the constraints of iterative training analysis: short series ($T{=}5$--$20$), non-stationarity by design, and heterogeneous method sensitivities.

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

\paragraph{Methodological pitfalls.}
\label{sec:pitfalls}
Lead-lag analysis in iterative model collapse is fragile along three axes, each documented with data from \S\ref{sec:regime}--\ref{sec:dose_response}.
\emph{Method sensitivity}: five detection methods applied to identical data ($\alpha{=}1.0$, 8 validated canary$\to$downstream pairs, direction-checked) yield forward significance rates spanning 0\% to 75\%, with inter-method agreement at $\kappa{=}0.185$ and naive cross-correlation reaching 75\% null-control FPR.
\emph{Spurious regression}: first-differencing to remove shared trends~\cite{granger1974spurious} eliminates canary$\to$perplexity associations ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$) while preserving canary$\to$diversity (24/24$\to$24/24), exposing an entire analysis channel as trend-driven rather than temporally precedent.
\emph{Regime dependence}: the same Granger test finds 0/8 pairs significant through $\alpha{=}0.45$ but 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$, a categorical shift at a 5-percentage-point boundary that a single-$\alpha$ study would miss entirely.
These pitfalls motivate systematic method comparison rather than reliance on any single detection approach.

\paragraph{Multi-Method Consensus Test (MMCT).}
\label{sec:mmct}
We apply the Multi-Method Consensus Test, a weighted consensus framework in the specification curve~\cite{simonsohn2020specification} and multi-method early-warning~\cite{scheffer2009early,bell2022modeling} traditions, adapted to the constraints of iterative training analysis: short series ($T{=}5$--$20$), non-stationarity by design, and heterogeneous method sensitivities.
MMCT is a consensus testing protocol, not a novel statistical method.
It compares five lead-lag detection methods through FPR-inverse weighted consensus, calibrated against null-control ($\alpha{=}0.0$) data where any detection is a false positive.
Each method $m_k$ receives weight $w_k = 1/\max(\hat{\text{FPR}}_k, \epsilon)$ with $\epsilon{=}0.01$; the weighted score $W(X \to Y) = \sum_k w_k d_k / \sum_k w_k$ yields formal $p$-values from the empirical null distribution (Appendix).
MMCT identifies permutation Granger (PermG) as the only method combining zero null-control FPR with consistent detection across contamination levels, and we recommend it as the primary detection method based on this systematic comparison.

\paragraph{Permutation Granger causality.}
PermG tests whether past values of canary metric $X$ improve prediction of downstream metric $Y$ beyond $Y$'s own history; Granger precedence establishes temporal predictive improvement, not true causality~\cite{shojaie2022granger}.
We apply 5{,}000 permutations~\citep{phipson2010permutation} on first-differenced series with Benjamini--Hochberg FDR correction at $q{=}0.05$ across 8 validated canary$\to$downstream pairs (2 canaries $\times$ 4 downstream metrics).
Three properties distinguish PermG: a nonparametric null distribution robust to the short non-stationary series typical of iterative training~\cite{boettiger2012limits}, built-in directionality (forward and reverse tested separately), and a hyperparameter-free test statistic.
The remaining four methods each exhibit a specific limitation: naive cross-correlation has 75\% null-control FPR; differenced cross-correlation detects bidirectionally without directional separation; threshold onset is power-limited at $T{=}11$ under corrected $3\sigma$ calibration (0/8 significant in 8 of 12 cross-architecture conditions); Toda--Yamamoto~\cite{toda1995statistical} achieves moderate supplementary detection (3--4/8 at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$) with reduced power from degree-of-freedom costs of lag augmentation.
Per-method dose-response profiles, Shapley value analysis, and the full MMCT algorithm appear in the Appendix.

\subsection{Signal-Times-Resolution Framework}
\label{sec:theory}

We apply standard statistical power scaling to PermG under the Signal$\times$Resolution (S$\times$R) framework.
Detectability of canary$\to$downstream temporal precedence depends on two competing factors:
\begin{equation}
    \text{Detectability}(\alpha) \;\propto\; S(\alpha) \times R(\alpha),
    \label{eq:detectability}
\end{equation}
where $S(\alpha)$ is signal strength (magnitude of distributional shift, monotonically increasing with $\alpha$) and $R(\alpha)$ is temporal resolution (the generational gap between canary and downstream responses).
$R(\alpha)$ is non-monotonic: at low $\alpha$, entropy and diversity respond in different generations ($R$ large); at $\alpha{\approx}0.60$, relaxation time matching compresses both responses into a single generation ($R \to 0$); at high $\alpha$, the severity of entropy collapse outpaces the diversity cascade, restoring the generational offset.
The product $S \times R$ predicts four regimes: \emph{blind} ($\alpha \leq 0.45$; $S$ below detection floor), \emph{onset} ($\alpha \approx 0.50$; $S$ crosses threshold while $R$ remains high), \emph{synchronous dip} ($\alpha \approx 0.60$; $R \to 0$ suppresses detection despite rising $S$), and \emph{detection} ($\alpha \geq 0.75$; $S$ dominates).
Full empirical confirmation appears in \S\ref{sec:regime} and \S\ref{sec:dose_response}.

Under a permutation test framework, detection power scales as $\mathrm{Power}(\alpha, T) = \Phi\bigl(S \cdot R \cdot \sqrt{T} / \sigma_{\mathrm{noise}}\bigr)$, where $\Phi$ is the standard normal CDF and the $\sqrt{T}$ scaling follows standard power analysis.
This instantiates the standard $z$-test power formula; the contribution is the empirical decomposition into signal $S(\alpha)$ and resolution $R(\alpha)$ components and the identification of $R(\alpha)$ non-monotonicity.
The detection phase transition at $\alpha_c$ (at $T{=}10$) is consistent with a power threshold: when $S \cdot R \cdot \sqrt{T}$ first exceeds the detection floor, power undergoes a steep onset from near-zero to near-one.
This generates three predictions for $T{=}20$: (i)~$\alpha_c$ left-shifts as increased $T$ raises power at all $\alpha$; (ii)~the transition smooths as $\sqrt{T}$ broadens the power curve; (iii)~different methods exhibit different $\alpha_c$ values due to method-specific power curves.
Bootstrap calibration ($N{=}10{,}000$) yields clean falsifiable tests at $\alpha{\geq}0.75$: predicted 7/8 (95\% CI: [6,8]); results below 6/8 would falsify $\sqrt{T}$ power scaling.
At $\alpha{=}0.45$, the point prediction is 0/8, but the bootstrap CI spans [0,7] reflecting $\alpha_c$ uncertainty---both detection and non-detection are informative for constraining the phase boundary location.
At $\alpha{=}0.50$, the prediction is inherently uncertain at the transition (CI: [0,7]).
Sub-threshold FDR $p{=}0.059$--$0.091$ at $\alpha{=}0.45$ is consistent with proximity to the power boundary.

\paragraph{Calibration.}
We validate error rates with built-in experimental controls.
False positive rate: at $\alpha{=}0.0$ (null control, no synthetic contamination), PermG and MMCT weighted consensus both yield 0\% FPR across 3 seeds (0/24 pairs at consensus $K{\geq}3$).
False negative rate: at $\alpha{=}1.0$, all 6 effect-size reference pairs (2 canaries $\times$ 3 diversity metrics, selected by criteria independent of the detection methods) are recovered at 0\% FNR across 4 seeds.
PermG matches consensus performance at all tested contamination levels, with cross-architecture validation confirming PermG forward significance ${\geq}6/8$ in 13 of 15 conditions (\S\ref{sec:generalization}).

4	\subsection{Experimental Setup}
5	\label{sec:setup}
6	
7	We study lead-lag analysis pitfalls in iterative training collapse using Pythia-410M \cite{biderman2023pythia}, a 410M-parameter decoder-only language model.
8	Pythia provides a controlled setting: small enough for multi-seed experiments across thirteen contamination levels, yet large enough to exhibit meaningful generation-over-generation degradation.

10	Training data is drawn from WikiText-103 \cite{merity2017pointer}, using 5{,}000-sample subsets per generation.
11	
12	Our protocol follows the replace paradigm of \citet{shumailov2024curse}, adapted for mixed synthetic-real training at $\alpha{<}1.0$.
13	Each generation $t$ proceeds in three steps: (1)~fine-tune the generation-$(t{-}1)$ model for 5{,}000 steps on a mixture of $\alpha$ fraction synthetic data and $(1{-}\alpha)$ fraction real data (AdamW optimizer, learning rate $5 \times 10^{-5}$, 500 warmup steps, weight decay $0.01$, batch size 4 for Pythia-410M, 32 for GPT-2-medium); (2)~generate 5{,}000 synthetic samples from the fine-tuned model (temperature $1.0$, top-$k{=}50$, max length 512 tokens); (3)~fully replace the synthetic pool.
14	We run $T{=}10$ generations (11 time points including the generation-0 baseline) across six primary contamination levels $\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00\}$ with multi-seed replication, plus five single-seed probing points ($\alpha \in \{0.05, 0.30, 0.35, 0.40, 0.55\}$) and two dual-seed fp32 probing points ($\alpha \in \{0.45, 0.60\}$) to resolve the onset boundary, yielding a 13-point $\alpha$ grid.

16	
17	We track two \emph{canary metrics} (cheap-to-compute statistics hypothesized to precede downstream degradation, inspired by early-warning signals in dynamical systems \cite{scheffer2009early}) and three \emph{downstream metrics}.
18	Canary metrics are token entropy (next-token prediction entropy averaged over held-out samples) and expected calibration error (ECE).
19	Downstream metrics are distinct-1 and distinct-2 ($n$-gram diversity \cite{li2016diversity}, computed over all 5{,}000 generated samples per generation) and perplexity (evaluated on held-out real data).
20	Token entropy is the mean next-token prediction entropy $H(p_\theta | \text{context})$ averaged over 1{,}000 held-out samples; ECE uses 15 equal-width bins.
21	We additionally evaluate effective rank and Self-BLEU as candidate canaries (Appendix).
22	Results for distinct-3 are reported in Appendix~\ref{app:distinct3}.
23	Code and data will be released upon publication.
24

26	Permutation Granger causality tests use 5{,}000 permutations on first-differenced series \cite{shojaie2022granger}.

31	\subsection{Detection Phase Transition}
32	\label{sec:regime}
33	
34	Diversity collapse occurs at every contamination level: distinct-1 declines by $14.1\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.0$ (fine-tuning drift) and by $40.3{\pm}0.3\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (3-seed mean).
35	Despite this ubiquitous degradation, Granger-causal detectability is sharply regime-dependent.
36	Permutation Granger (PermG) tests find 0/8 canary$\to$downstream pairs FDR-significant from $\alpha{=}0.00$ through $\alpha{=}0.45$, then jump to 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (2~fp32 seeds, consistent).
37	This transition is striking because cumulative synthetic fraction barely changes across the boundary: $C = 1{-}(1{-}\alpha)^{10}$ yields $99.75\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.45$ versus $99.90\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.50$, a difference of 0.15 percentage points, yet detection jumps from null to reliable.
38	Sigmoid regression across the 13-point $\alpha$ grid quantifies this steep onset: $\alpha_c = 0.476$ (bootstrap 95\% CI: [0.43, 0.56]), steepness $k \geq 200$, transition width $\Delta\alpha \approx 0.02$ (CI: [0.008, 0.060]), $R^2 = 0.969$ (versus power-law $R^2 = 0.808$, $\Delta\mathrm{AIC} = 18.2$; Figure~\ref{fig:regime_map}).

40	A model-free Fisher exact test corroborates the categorical jump: 0/64 pairs FDR-significant at $\alpha \leq 0.45$ versus 18/32 at $\alpha \geq 0.50$ ($p = 3.45 \times 10^{-11}$).

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

\subsection{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

We study lead-lag analysis pitfalls in iterative training collapse using Pythia-410M \cite{biderman2023pythia}, a 410M-parameter decoder-only language model.
Pythia provides a controlled setting: small enough for multi-seed experiments across thirteen contamination levels, yet large enough to exhibit meaningful generation-over-generation degradation.
Cross-architecture validation uses GPT-2-medium (345M parameters, also decoder-only), a second transformer family of similar scale; results are reported in \S\ref{sec:regime} and \S\ref{sec:discussion}.
Training data is drawn from WikiText-103 \cite{merity2017pointer}, using 5{,}000-sample subsets per generation.

Our protocol follows the replace paradigm of \citet{shumailov2024curse}, adapted for mixed synthetic-real training at $\alpha{<}1.0$.
Each generation $t$ proceeds in three steps: (1)~fine-tune the generation-$(t{-}1)$ model for 5{,}000 steps on a mixture of $\alpha$ fraction synthetic data and $(1{-}\alpha)$ fraction real data (AdamW optimizer, learning rate $5 \times 10^{-5}$, 500 warmup steps, weight decay $0.01$, batch size 4 for Pythia-410M, 32 for GPT-2-medium); (2)~generate 5{,}000 synthetic samples from the fine-tuned model (temperature $1.0$, top-$k{=}50$, max length 512 tokens); (3)~fully replace the synthetic pool.
We run $T{=}10$ generations (11 time points including the generation-0 baseline) across six primary contamination levels $\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00\}$ with multi-seed replication, plus five single-seed probing points ($\alpha \in \{0.05, 0.30, 0.35, 0.40, 0.55\}$) and two dual-seed fp32 probing points ($\alpha \in \{0.45, 0.60\}$) to resolve the onset boundary, yielding a 13-point $\alpha$ grid.
The $\alpha{=}1.0$ condition uses four random seeds $\{42, 43, 44, 45\}$; $\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75\}$ each use three seeds $\{42, 43, 44\}$; $\alpha \in \{0.45, 0.60\}$ each use two seeds $\{42, 43\}$; remaining levels use a single seed (42).

We track two \emph{canary metrics} (cheap-to-compute statistics hypothesized to precede downstream degradation, inspired by early-warning signals in dynamical systems \cite{scheffer2009early}) and three \emph{downstream metrics}.
Canary metrics are token entropy (next-token prediction entropy averaged over held-out samples) and expected calibration error (ECE).
Downstream metrics are distinct-1 and distinct-2 ($n$-gram diversity \cite{li2016diversity}, computed over all 5{,}000 generated samples per generation) and perplexity (evaluated on held-out real data).
Token entropy is the mean next-token prediction entropy $H(p_\theta | \text{context})$ averaged over 1{,}000 held-out samples; ECE uses 15 equal-width bins.
We additionally evaluate effective rank and Self-BLEU as candidate canaries (Appendix).
Results for distinct-3 are reported in Appendix~\ref{app:distinct3}.
Code and data will be released upon publication.

All hypothesis tests apply Benjamini--Hochberg (BH) FDR correction at $q{=}0.05$.
Permutation Granger causality tests use 5{,}000 permutations on first-differenced series \cite{shojaie2022granger}.
Cross-correlation analysis uses a maximum lag of 5 generations.
Raw metric drift from generation~0 to generation~10 is summarized in Appendix Table~\ref{tab:drift_summary}.


\subsection{Detection Phase Transition}
\label{sec:regime}

Diversity collapse occurs at every contamination level: distinct-1 declines by $14.1\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.0$ (fine-tuning drift) and by $40.3{\pm}0.3\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (3-seed mean).
Despite this ubiquitous degradation, Granger-causal detectability is sharply regime-dependent.
Permutation Granger (PermG) tests find 0/8 canary$\to$downstream pairs FDR-significant from $\alpha{=}0.00$ through $\alpha{=}0.45$, then jump to 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (2~fp32 seeds, consistent).
This transition is striking because cumulative synthetic fraction barely changes across the boundary: $C = 1{-}(1{-}\alpha)^{10}$ yields $99.75\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.45$ versus $99.90\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.50$, a difference of 0.15 percentage points, yet detection jumps from null to reliable.
Sigmoid regression across the 13-point $\alpha$ grid quantifies this steep onset: $\alpha_c = 0.476$ (bootstrap 95\% CI: [0.43, 0.56]), steepness $k \geq 200$, transition width $\Delta\alpha \approx 0.02$ (CI: [0.008, 0.060]), $R^2 = 0.969$ (versus power-law $R^2 = 0.808$, $\Delta\mathrm{AIC} = 18.2$; Figure~\ref{fig:regime_map}).
The wide confidence interval reflects estimation uncertainty in \emph{where} the boundary lies, not \emph{whether} it exists: the transition width $\Delta\alpha \approx 0.02$ is $6{\times}$ narrower than the CI, confirming a genuinely steep onset regardless of the exact boundary position.
A model-free Fisher exact test corroborates the categorical jump: 0/64 pairs FDR-significant at $\alpha \leq 0.45$ versus 18/32 at $\alpha \geq 0.50$ ($p = 3.45 \times 10^{-11}$).
At $\alpha{=}0.45$, PermG $p$-values reveal sub-threshold signal ($p_{\mathrm{fdr}} = 0.059$ for seed~43, $0.091$ for seed~42), consistent with the power-threshold interpretation of $\alpha_c$ at $T{=}10$ (\S\ref{sec:theory}): the onset reflects PermG's power curve crossing the detection floor, not the emergence of a new physical signal.
A specification curve analysis spanning 1{,}160 analytical specifications confirms that the detection phase transition is specification-invariant.

First-differencing scopes the canary claim precisely.
Canary$\to$diversity pairs retain unanimous FDR significance after first-differencing ($24/24 \to 24/24$ across 4~seeds at $\alpha{=}1.0$, 6 pairs per seed), while canary$\to$perplexity collapses entirely ($F \approx 0$, $p = 0.99$): the apparent perplexity association is a shared-trend artifact.
All canary claims are therefore scoped to diversity metrics only.
At $\alpha{=}1.0$, all 24 canary$\to$diversity pairs (6 per seed $\times$ 4~seeds; mauve excluded) reach FDR significance in the forward direction with 0/24 reverse; directional asymmetry is robust across all WikiText conditions.
The canary mechanism also exhibits a blind spot: at $\alpha{=}0.10$, distinct-1 has already dropped by $39.6\%$, yet token entropy is indistinguishable from the null ($-5.3\%$ versus $-4.6{\pm}0.4\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.0$).
Below $\alpha_c$ at $T{=}10$, diversity collapse proceeds without any detectable Granger-causal signal in the canary metrics.

\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/metric_trajectory.pdf}
\caption{Metric trajectories at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (Pythia-410M, 4~seeds). Token entropy drops at generation~1; distinct-1 declines from generations~2--3, with a consistent one-generation canary lead across all four seeds (shaded: inter-seed range). This pattern corresponds to 24/24 forward and 0/24 reverse FDR-significant canary$\to$diversity pairs (6 per seed, mauve excluded).}
\label{fig:metric_trajectory}
\end{figure}


\subsection{Dose-Response and the $S \times R$ Framework}
\label{sec:dose_response}

The PermG dose-response profile (Figure~\ref{fig:regime_map}) reveals four detection regimes: \emph{blind} ($\alpha \leq 0.45$, 0/8 FDR-significant pairs), \emph{onset} ($\alpha \approx 0.50$, 6/8), \emph{synchronous dip} ($\alpha \approx 0.60$, 0/8 both seeds; dual-seed confirmed), and \emph{detection} ($\alpha{=}0.75$, 0--6/8 per seed, 2 of 3 seeds ${\geq}5/8$; $\alpha{=}1.0$, 6/8 across 4~seeds).
The non-monotonic dip at $\alpha{=}0.60$ is consistent with the $S \times R$ framework (\S\ref{sec:theory}): signal strength $S(\alpha)$ rises monotonically with contamination, but temporal resolution $R(\alpha)$ drops when relaxation time approaches the observation interval.
At $\alpha \approx 0.60$, this compression drives the canary-to-downstream lag toward zero, and the product $S \times R$ reaches a local minimum.
The synchronous zone is mechanistically distinct from the blind spot: in the blind zone, canary drift is indistinguishable from the null; in the synchronous zone, both canary and downstream metrics drift substantially but without temporal offset.

Method choice is itself a major source of analytic variability.
At $\alpha{=}1.0$, direction-checked forward significance rates span 0\% to 75\%: naive and differenced cross-correlation fall to 0/8 after lag-direction filtering (all significant correlations peak at negative lags), while PermG achieves 6/8 (Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison}). Inter-method agreement is $\kappa{=}0.185$ (near chance).
PermG is the only method that combines zero null-control FPR with consistent detection at $\alpha \geq 0.50$ (Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison}); its nonparametric null distribution, built-in directionality, and hyperparameter-free design explain this advantage.
The $S \times R$ framework generates three testable predictions for $T{=}20$ via $\mathrm{Power}(\alpha, T) = \Phi(S \cdot R \cdot \sqrt{T}/\sigma)$: (i)~$\alpha_c$ at $T{=}10$ should left-shift, (ii)~the transition should smooth, and (iii)~different methods should exhibit different $\alpha_c$ values.
These predictions are under empirical verification.

\subsection{Cross-Architecture Generalization}
\label{sec:generalization}

We evaluate the detection phase transition across 15 model-seed combinations spanning six families (Pythia, GPT-2, OPT, Qwen, SmolLM3, Padding-variant), scales from 345M to 6.9B parameters, and two training domains (WikiText-103, C4).
Table~\ref{tab:generalization} reports PermG forward detection at $\alpha{=}1.0$.
PermG forward significance reaches ${\geq}$6/8 in 13 of 15 conditions (87\%).
Two exceptions emerge: Pythia-1.4B seed~42 on WikiText (2/8), a seed-dependent outlier that recovers to 6/8 in seed~43, and SmolLM3-3B (3/8), where only ECE$\to$downstream pairs reach significance while entropy$\to$downstream pairs fail entirely (0/4; details in Appendix).

The onset boundary $\alpha_c \approx 0.50$ at $T{=}10$ is architecture-independent: every family that achieves detection does so at or above this threshold, and none achieves reliable detection below it.

At Pythia-6.9B (bf16), detection recovers to 7/8 on WikiText.
Dataset characteristics modulate detection power independently of model capacity.

\subsection{Detection Phase Transition}
\label{sec:regime}

Diversity collapse occurs at every contamination level: distinct-1 declines by $14.1\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.0$ (fine-tuning drift) and by $40.3{\pm}0.3\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (3-seed mean).
Despite this ubiquitous degradation, Granger-causal detectability is sharply regime-dependent.
Permutation Granger (PermG) tests find 0/8 canary$\to$downstream pairs FDR-significant from $\alpha{=}0.00$ through $\alpha{=}0.45$, then jump to 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (2~fp32 seeds, consistent).
This transition is striking because cumulative synthetic fraction barely changes across the boundary: $C = 1{-}(1{-}\alpha)^{10}$ yields $99.75\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.45$ versus $99.90\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.50$, a difference of 0.15 percentage points, yet detection jumps from null to reliable.
Sigmoid regression across the 13-point $\alpha$ grid quantifies this steep onset: $\alpha_c = 0.476$ at $T{=}10$, steepness $k \geq 200$, transition width $\Delta\alpha \approx 0.02$, $R^2 = 0.969$ (versus power-law $R^2 = 0.808$, $\Delta\mathrm{AIC} = 18.2$; Figure~\ref{fig:phase_transition}).
At $\alpha{=}0.45$, PermG $p$-values reveal sub-threshold signal ($p_{\mathrm{fdr}} = 0.059$ for seed~43, $0.091$ for seed~42), consistent with the power-threshold interpretation of $\alpha_c$ at $T{=}10$ (\S\ref{sec:theory}): the onset reflects PermG's power curve crossing the detection floor, not the emergence of a new physical signal.
A specification curve analysis spanning 1{,}160 analytical specifications confirms that the detection phase transition is specification-invariant.

First-differencing scopes the canary claim precisely.
Canary$\to$diversity pairs retain unanimous FDR significance after first-differencing ($24/24 \to 24/24$ across 4~seeds at $\alpha{=}1.0$), while canary$\to$perplexity collapses entirely ($F \approx 0$, $p = 0.99$): the apparent perplexity association is a shared-trend artifact.
All canary claims are therefore scoped to diversity metrics only.
At $\alpha{=}1.0$, 24/24 forward-direction pairs reach FDR significance with 0/24 reverse (4~seeds); directional asymmetry is robust across all WikiText conditions.
The canary mechanism also exhibits a blind spot: at $\alpha{=}0.10$, distinct-1 has already dropped by $39.6\%$, yet token entropy is indistinguishable from the null ($-5.3\%$ versus $-4.6{\pm}0.4\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.0$).
Below $\alpha_c$ at $T{=}10$, diversity collapse proceeds without any detectable Granger-causal signal in the canary metrics.

This pattern corresponds to 24/24 forward and 0/24 reverse FDR-significant pairs.}

\subsection{Dose-Response and the $S \times R$ Framework}
\label{sec:dose_response}

The PermG dose-response profile (Figure~\ref{fig:regime_map}) reveals four detection regimes: \emph{blind} ($\alpha \leq 0.45$, 0/8 FDR-significant pairs), \emph{onset} ($\alpha \approx 0.50$, 6/8), \emph{synchronous dip} ($\alpha \approx 0.60$, 0/8 both seeds; dual-seed confirmed), and \emph{detection} ($\alpha \geq 0.75$, 5--6/8 per seed across 3~seeds; $\alpha{=}1.0$, 6/8 across 4~seeds).
The non-monotonic dip at $\alpha{=}0.60$ is consistent with the $S \times R$ framework (\S\ref{sec:theory}): signal strength $S(\alpha)$ rises monotonically with contamination, but temporal resolution $R(\alpha)$ drops when relaxation time approaches the observation interval.
At $\alpha \approx 0.60$, this compression drives the canary-to-downstream lag toward zero, and the product $S \times R$ reaches a local minimum.
The synchronous zone is mechanistically distinct from the blind spot: in the blind zone, canary drift is indistinguishable from the null; in the synchronous zone, both canary and downstream metrics drift substantially but without temporal offset.

Method choice is itself a major source of analytic variability.
At $\alpha{=}1.0$, forward-direction significance rates range from 100\% (naive cross-correlation) to 37.5\% (PermG), with inter-method $\kappa = 0.185$ (near chance) and a spurious rate of at least 62.5\%.
PermG is the only method that combines zero null-control FPR with consistent detection at $\alpha \geq 0.50$ (Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison}); its nonparametric null distribution, built-in directionality, and hyperparameter-free design explain this advantage.
The $S \times R$ framework generates three testable predictions for $T{=}20$ via $\mathrm{Power}(\alpha, T) = \Phi(S \cdot R \cdot \sqrt{T}/\sigma)$: (i)~$\alpha_c$ at $T{=}10$ should left-shift, (ii)~the transition should smooth, and (iii)~different methods should exhibit different $\alpha_c$ values.
These predictions are under empirical verification.

\subsection{Cross-Architecture Generalization}
\label{sec:generalization}

We evaluate the detection phase transition across 15 model-seed combinations spanning six families (Pythia, GPT-2, OPT, Qwen, SmolLM3, Padding-variant), scales from 345M to 6.9B parameters, and two training domains (WikiText-103, C4).

PermG forward significance reaches ${\geq}$6/8 in 13 of 15 conditions (87\%).
Two exceptions emerge: Pythia-1.4B seed~42 on WikiText (2/8), a seed-dependent outlier that recovers to 6/8 in seed~43, and SmolLM3-3B (3/8), where only ECE$\to$downstream pairs reach significance while entropy$\to$downstream pairs fail entirely (0/4; details in Appendix).
SmolLM3's token entropy exhibits non-monotonic oscillations across generations; this pattern violates the monotonic decline that Granger tests require.
The onset boundary $\alpha_c \approx 0.50$ at $T{=}10$ is architecture-independent: every family that achieves detection does so at or above this threshold, and none achieves reliable detection below it.

Replacing WikiText-103 with C4 yields the strongest detection observed: Pythia-1B reaches PermG~fwd 8/8 (2~seeds), and Pythia-1.4B reaches 8/8 on C4 versus 2/8 on WikiText at the same scale.
At Pythia-6.9B (bf16), detection recovers to 7/8 on WikiText.
Dataset characteristics modulate detection power independently of model capacity.
Directional asymmetry also varies by domain: at $\alpha{=}0.50$ on C4, PermG reverse reaches 7/8, compared to 0/24 across all WikiText conditions.
This domain-dependent bidirectionality suggests that the unidirectional forward causation observed on WikiText may partly reflect domain-specific dynamics (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

296	\section{Sequential Monitoring: CUSUM vs Calibrated Threshold}
297	\label{app:csmp}
298	
299	We translate the Granger-precedence finding into a deployable monitoring protocol using CUSUM (cumulative sum) sequential testing, calibrated against the $\alpha{=}0.0$ null control.
300	The null-calibration procedure sets the alarm threshold $h$ such that the false alarm rate (FAR) is 0\% on null data (3~seeds, $T{=}10$), providing controlled Type~I error guarantees.
301	
302	\paragraph{Method.}
303	CUSUM monitors the cumulative deviation of token entropy from its null-control baseline: $S_t = \max(0,\; S_{t-1} + (\mu_0 - x_t) - k)$, where $\mu_0$ is the null-control mean, $k$ is the allowance parameter, and the alarm triggers when $S_t > h$.

355	\section{Background and Notation}
356	\label{app:background}
357	\label{sec:background}
358	
359	This section establishes the formal setup and notation used throughout the paper.
360	
361	\paragraph{Iterative training loop.}
362	Let $M_0$ denote a pretrained language model and $\mathcal{D}_\text{real}$ a fixed corpus of human-written text.
363	At each generation $t \geq 1$, the model $M_{t-1}$ generates a synthetic corpus $\mathcal{D}_\text{synth}^{(t-1)}$, and the next-generation model $M_t$ is fine-tuned on a mixture of $\alpha$ fraction synthetic data and $(1{-}\alpha)$ fraction real data:
364	\begin{equation}
365	    \mathcal{D}_\text{train}^{(t)} = \alpha \cdot \mathcal{D}_\text{synth}^{(t-1)} \;+\; (1{-}\alpha) \cdot \mathcal{D}_\text{real}, \quad \alpha \in [0, 1].
366	    \label{eq:mixing}
367	\end{equation}
368	At $\alpha{=}1.0$, this reduces to the full-replacement paradigm of \citet{shumailov2024curse}.
369	
370	\paragraph{Metric families.}
371	\emph{Canary metrics}: token entropy ($H(p_\theta | \text{context})$ on held-out samples) and expected calibration error (ECE).
372	\emph{Downstream metrics}: distinct-$n$ ($n \in \{1, 2, 3\}$)~\cite{li2016diversity} and perplexity.
373	Each metric produces a time series of $T{+}1$ observations.
374	
375	\paragraph{Lead-lag testing.}
376	Given canary series $X$ and downstream series $Y$, the central question is whether changes in $X$ temporally precede changes in $Y$, requiring directionality and confounder control beyond simple correlation.
377	We employ five methods spanning permissive to conservative: naive cross-correlation, differenced cross-correlation, threshold onset detection, permutation Granger causality~\cite{shojaie2022granger}, and Toda--Yamamoto Granger causality~\cite{toda1995statistical}.
378	
379	\section{MMCT Algorithm}
380	\label{app:mmct}
381	
382	Algorithm~\ref{alg:mmct} describes the Multi-Method Consensus Test (MMCT) introduced in \S\ref{sec:mmct}.
383	
384	\begin{algorithm}[h]
385	\caption{Multi-Method Consensus Test (MMCT)}
386	\label{alg:mmct}
387	\begin{algorithmic}[1]
388	\Require Time series pair $(X, Y)$; methods $\{m_1, \ldots, m_K\}$ ($K{=}5$); null-control data $\mathcal{N}$ (from $\alpha{=}0.0$); tolerance $\epsilon{=}0.01$
389	\Ensure $p$-value, consensus level $\hat{K}$
390	\For{each method $m_k$}
391	    \State Compute empirical FPR: $\widehat{\mathrm{FPR}}_k \gets$ fraction of null-control pairs where $m_k$ rejects $H_0$
392	    \State Compute weight: $w_k \gets 1 / \max(\widehat{\mathrm{FPR}}_k,\; \epsilon)$
393	    \State Apply $m_k$ to $(X, Y)$: $d_k \gets \mathbf{1}[m_k \text{ rejects } H_0]$
394	\EndFor
395	\State Weighted consensus: $W(X {\to} Y) \gets \sum_{k} w_k \, d_k \;/\; \sum_{k} w_k$
396	\State Build empirical null distribution of $W$ from all null-control pairs in $\mathcal{N}$
397	\State Compute $p$-value from empirical null: $p \gets \Pr_{\mathcal{N}}(W \geq W_{\mathrm{obs}})$
398	\State Consensus level: $\hat{K} \gets \sum_{k} d_k$
399	\State \Return $p$, $\hat{K}$
400	\end{algorithmic}
401	\end{algorithm}
402	
403	\paragraph{Design rationale.}
404	FPR-inverse weighting penalizes methods with high false positive rates on null-control data: naive cross-correlation (FPR${=}75\%$) receives weight $w{=}1.33$, while PermG (FPR${=}0\%$) receives $w{=}100$ (capped by $\epsilon$).
405	The empirical null distribution avoids parametric assumptions that are unreliable for short ($T{=}5$--$20$), non-stationary series typical of iterative training.
406	MMCT is a consensus testing protocol, not a novel statistical method; its value lies in systematic method comparison and the identification of method-dependent conclusions.

437	\section{Extended Discussion}
438	\label{app:extended_discussion}
439	
440	\paragraph{Calibration scope and generalization.}
441	All FPR and FNR calibration results are specific to our experimental setup: Pythia-410M, WikiText-103 subset, $T{=}10$, and six contamination levels.
442	Cross-architecture validation across 15 confirmed conditions spanning six model families confirms that the entropy-leads-diversity pattern generalizes: PermG forward significance reaches ${\geq}6/8$ in 13 of 15 architecture-seed combinations (Table~\ref{tab:generalization}); SmolLM3-3B (3/8) diverges due to canary metric splitting.
443	
444	\paragraph{Domain-dependent directionality.}
445	The unidirectional forward causation observed on WikiText (PermG reverse${=}$0/8 across all conditions) does not hold universally.
446	On C4 at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (s42 fp32), PermG reverse reaches 7/8, indicating near-symmetric bidirectional coupling; however, this is seed-dependent (s43: 1/8) and noted as preliminary.
447	The practical implication is that directional asymmetry should be verified per domain.
448	
449	\paragraph{Token entropy versus perplexity.}
450	The distinction lies in the evaluation domain: token entropy is $H(p_\theta | \text{context})$ on held-out real data, while perplexity is $\exp(H_\text{cross})$ on model-generated text.
451	First-differencing removes their shared downward trend: the canary$\to$diversity channel survives because entropy leads diversity by one generation, whereas the canary$\to$perplexity channel vanishes because both co-move synchronously.
452	
453	\paragraph{NLP-specific constraints.}
454	Our application of Granger-type methods faces constraints absent in econometrics: (i)~observation length ($T{=}5$--$20$ vs.\ $T{=}100$--$1000$); (ii)~non-stationarity by design rather than incidental; (iii)~small multiplicity for FDR correction (8--32 pairs per regime).
455	Transfer entropy (0/192 FDR-significant results) confirms that method sensitivity extends beyond the five-method panel.
456	
457	\paragraph{Prevention paradox.}
458	Effective intervention truncates the collapse trajectory that established Granger precedence.
459	Differenced cross-correlation retains significance under intervention (31/32 pairs), while threshold onset fails entirely (0/8), reinforcing the multi-method rationale.
460	
461	\paragraph{Canary metric choice.}
462	SmolLM3-3B reveals that canary metric selection constitutes a sensitivity dimension beyond the five statistical methods: token entropy exhibits non-monotonic oscillations (0/4 significant pairs), while ECE maintains monotonic growth (3/4 pairs).
463	No single canary metric is universally optimal.
464	
465	\paragraph{Future work.}
466	Extensions include multivariate VAR models for confounder testing, multi-seed replication across all six architecture families, longer training runs ($T{\geq}20$), online monitoring within training pipelines, and accumulate-mode experiments~\cite{dey2024breaking}.
467	The sigmoid onset boundary ($\alpha_c{=}0.476$) invites connection to the critical mixture ratio scaling law of \citet{gu2024cmr} and the data-mixing phase transitions of \citet{gu2025datamixing}.

This instability reflects bimodal lag distributions (modes at lag~1 and lag~3--4), suggesting that distinct-3 captures two temporally distinct diversity loss mechanisms: rapid n-gram homogenization (lag~1) and slower distributional narrowing (lag~3--4).

\paragraph{Sensitivity to sequence length.}
Higher-order $n$-gram diversity metrics are more sensitive to generation length and random sampling variability.
With our 512-token generation length, distinct-3 has a smaller effective denominator (number of possible unique trigrams observed) than distinct-1 or distinct-2, amplifying stochastic fluctuations.
This partially explains the higher lag instability: the signal-to-noise ratio for temporal precedence is lower for distinct-3, requiring more observations (longer $T$ or more seeds) to achieve stable estimates.
For this reason, we report distinct-3 in this appendix rather than in the main text, where distinct-1 and distinct-2 provide cleaner evidence of the entropy-leads-diversity pattern.

\section{Change-Point Detection Analysis}
\label{app:change_point}

We apply a max-split change-point test with bootstrap significance assessment ($n{=}5{,}000$, $p{<}0.05$) to each metric's generation-level time series ($T{=}11$).

Under the null control ($\alpha{=}0.00$, 3~seeds), downstream diversity metrics (distinct-1, distinct-2, distinct-3) produce significant change-points at generation~2 in all seeds (9/9 tests). With additional significant tests from ECE (2/3 seeds) and token entropy (1/3 seeds), the overall false positive rate reaches 66.7\% (12/18 tests; Table~\ref{tab:cp_null}). The monotonic drift inherent in iterative self-training is sufficient to trigger change-point detection even without canary contamination. Individual change-point significance therefore cannot serve as standalone evidence for a canary-specific effect.

Although individual significance is unreliable as a discriminator, the temporal ordering of detected change-points reverses between null and treatment conditions. In the null ($\alpha{=}0.00$), downstream metrics show the earliest significant breaks at generation~2 (all seeds), while significant canary breaks appear later (ECE at generations~4--8). Under treatment conditions ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$), this ordering flips: canary metrics place their best splits at generation~1, followed by downstream diversity metrics at generations~2--4 and perplexity at generation~4 (Table~\ref{tab:cp_results}). This ordering reversal provides complementary evidence from a distinct statistical framework, consistent with the Granger causality analysis in \S\ref{sec:experiments}.

Several caveats apply. The 18 individual tests per condition were not corrected for multiple comparisons (BH or Bonferroni); primary inference rests on the cross-metric temporal ordering rather than on individual significance tests. Under treatment conditions, token entropy places its best split at generation~1 with large effect sizes ($|d|{>}2.5$) in all seeds, but the pre-change segment at a generation-1 split contains only a single data point, reducing bootstrap power (1/3 seeds significant at $\alpha{=}0.75$). The short series length ($T{=}11$) further limits overall detection power.

\section{Sequential Monitoring: CUSUM vs Calibrated Threshold}
\label{app:csmp}

We translate the Granger-precedence finding into a deployable monitoring protocol using CUSUM (cumulative sum) sequential testing, calibrated against the $\alpha{=}0.0$ null control.
The null-calibration procedure sets the alarm threshold $h$ such that the false alarm rate (FAR) is 0\% on null data (3~seeds, $T{=}10$), providing controlled Type~I error guarantees.

\paragraph{Method.}
CUSUM monitors the cumulative deviation of token entropy from its null-control baseline: $S_t = \max(0,\; S_{t-1} + (\mu_0 - x_t) - k)$, where $\mu_0$ is the null-control mean, $k$ is the allowance parameter, and the alarm triggers when $S_t > h$.
We calibrate $h$ for each $k$ from the $\alpha{=}0.0$ null data (Table~\ref{tab:csmp_calibration}).
As a baseline, we compare against a simple calibrated threshold: alarm when the metric crosses $\mu_0 - 2\sigma_0$ for $n{\geq}1$ or $n{\geq}2$ consecutive generations.

\section{Background and Notation}
\label{app:background}
\label{sec:background}

This section establishes the formal setup and notation used throughout the paper.

\paragraph{Iterative training loop.}
Let $M_0$ denote a pretrained language model and $\mathcal{D}_\text{real}$ a fixed corpus of human-written text.
At each generation $t \geq 1$, the model $M_{t-1}$ generates a synthetic corpus $\mathcal{D}_\text{synth}^{(t-1)}$, and the next-generation model $M_t$ is fine-tuned on a mixture of $\alpha$ fraction synthetic data and $(1{-}\alpha)$ fraction real data:
\begin{equation}
    \mathcal{D}_\text{train}^{(t)} = \alpha \cdot \mathcal{D}_\text{synth}^{(t-1)} \;+\; (1{-}\alpha) \cdot \mathcal{D}_\text{real}, \quad \alpha \in [0, 1].
    \label{eq:mixing}
\end{equation}
At $\alpha{=}1.0$, this reduces to the full-replacement paradigm of \citet{shumailov2024curse}.

\paragraph{Metric families.}
\emph{Canary metrics}: token entropy ($H(p_\theta | \text{context})$ on held-out samples) and expected calibration error (ECE).
\emph{Downstream metrics}: distinct-$n$ ($n \in \{1, 2, 3\}$)~\cite{li2016diversity} and perplexity.
Each metric produces a time series of $T{+}1$ observations.

\paragraph{Lead-lag testing.}
Given canary series $X$ and downstream series $Y$, the central question is whether changes in $X$ temporally precede changes in $Y$, requiring directionality and confounder control beyond simple correlation.
We employ five methods spanning permissive to conservative: naive cross-correlation, differenced cross-correlation, threshold onset detection, permutation Granger causality~\cite{shojaie2022granger}, and Toda--Yamamoto Granger causality~\cite{toda1995statistical}.

\section{MMCT Algorithm}
\label{app:mmct}

Algorithm~\ref{alg:mmct} describes the Multi-Method Consensus Test (MMCT) introduced in \S\ref{sec:mmct}.

\begin{algorithm}[h]
\caption{Multi-Method Consensus Test (MMCT)}
\label{alg:mmct}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\Require Time series pair $(X, Y)$; methods $\{m_1, \ldots, m_K\}$ ($K{=}5$); null-control data $\mathcal{N}$ (from $\alpha{=}0.0$); tolerance $\epsilon{=}0.01$
\Ensure $p$-value, consensus level $\hat{K}$
\For{each method $m_k$}
    \State Compute empirical FPR: $\widehat{\mathrm{FPR}}_k \gets$ fraction of null-control pairs where $m_k$ rejects $H_0$
    \State Compute weight: $w_k \gets 1 / \max(\widehat{\mathrm{FPR}}_k,\; \epsilon)$
    \State Apply $m_k$ to $(X, Y)$: $d_k \gets \mathbf{1}[m_k \text{ rejects } H_0]$
\EndFor
\State Weighted consensus: $W(X {\to} Y) \gets \sum_{k} w_k \, d_k \;/\; \sum_{k} w_k$
\State Build empirical null distribution of $W$ from all null-control pairs in $\mathcal{N}$
\State Compute $p$-value from empirical null: $p \gets \Pr_{\mathcal{N}}(W \geq W_{\mathrm{obs}})$
\State Consensus level: $\hat{K} \gets \sum_{k} d_k$
\State \Return $p$, $\hat{K}$
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\paragraph{Design rationale.}
FPR-inverse weighting penalizes methods with high false positive rates on null-control data: naive cross-correlation (FPR${=}75\%$) receives weight $w{=}1.33$, while PermG (FPR${=}0\%$) receives $w{=}100$ (capped by $\epsilon$).
The empirical null distribution avoids parametric assumptions that are unreliable for short ($T{=}5$--$20$), non-stationary series typical of iterative training.
MMCT is a consensus testing protocol, not a novel statistical method; its value lies in systematic method comparison and the identification of method-dependent conclusions.

\section{Extended Discussion}
\label{app:extended_discussion}

\paragraph{Calibration scope and generalization.}
All FPR and FNR calibration results are specific to our experimental setup: Pythia-410M, WikiText-103 subset, $T{=}10$, and six contamination levels.
Cross-architecture validation across 15 confirmed conditions spanning six model families confirms that the entropy-leads-diversity pattern generalizes: PermG forward significance reaches ${\geq}6/8$ in 13 of 15 architecture-seed combinations (Table~\ref{tab:generalization}); SmolLM3-3B (3/8) diverges due to canary metric splitting.

\paragraph{Domain-dependent directionality.}
The unidirectional forward causation observed on WikiText (PermG reverse${=}$0/8 across all conditions) does not hold universally.
On C4 at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (s42 fp32), PermG reverse reaches 7/8, indicating near-symmetric bidirectional coupling; however, this is seed-dependent (s43: 1/8) and noted as preliminary.
The practical implication is that directional asymmetry should be verified per domain.

\paragraph{Token entropy versus perplexity.}
The distinction lies in the evaluation domain: token entropy is $H(p_\theta | \text{context})$ on held-out real data, while perplexity is $\exp(H_\text{cross})$ on model-generated text.
First-differencing removes their shared downward trend: the canary$\to$diversity channel survives because entropy leads diversity by one generation, whereas the canary$\to$perplexity channel vanishes because both co-move synchronously.

\paragraph{NLP-specific constraints.}

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

\paragraph{Methodological pitfalls.}
\label{sec:pitfalls}
Lead-lag analysis in iterative model collapse is fragile along three axes, each documented with data from \S\ref{sec:regime}--\ref{sec:dose_response}.
\emph{Method sensitivity}: five detection methods applied to identical data ($\alpha{=}1.0$, 8 validated canary$\to$downstream pairs, direction-checked) yield forward significance rates spanning 0\% to 75\%, with inter-method agreement at $\kappa{=}0.185$ and naive cross-correlation reaching 75\% null-control FPR.
\emph{Spurious regression}: first-differencing to remove shared trends~\cite{granger1974spurious} eliminates canary$\to$perplexity associations ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$) while preserving canary$\to$diversity (24/24$\to$24/24), exposing an entire analysis channel as trend-driven rather than temporally precedent.
\emph{Regime dependence}: the same Granger test finds 0/8 pairs significant through $\alpha{=}0.45$ but 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$, a categorical shift at a 5-percentage-point boundary that a single-$\alpha$ study would miss entirely.
These pitfalls motivate systematic method comparison rather than reliance on any single detection approach.

\paragraph{Multi-Method Consensus Test (MMCT).}
\label{sec:mmct}
We apply the Multi-Method Consensus Test, a weighted consensus framework in the specification curve~\cite{simonsohn2020specification} and multi-method early-warning~\cite{scheffer2009early,bell2022modeling} traditions, adapted to the constraints of iterative training analysis: short series ($T{=}5$--$20$), non-stationarity by design, and heterogeneous method sensitivities.
MMCT is a consensus testing protocol, not a novel statistical method.
It compares five lead-lag detection methods through FPR-inverse weighted consensus, calibrated against null-control ($\alpha{=}0.0$) data where any detection is a false positive.
Each method $m_k$ receives weight $w_k = 1/\max(\hat{\text{FPR}}_k, \epsilon)$ with $\epsilon{=}0.01$; the weighted score $W(X \to Y) = \sum_k w_k d_k / \sum_k w_k$ yields formal $p$-values from the empirical null distribution (Appendix).
MMCT identifies permutation Granger (PermG) as the only method combining zero null-control FPR with consistent detection across contamination levels, and we recommend it as the primary detection method based on this systematic comparison.

\paragraph{Permutation Granger causality.}
PermG tests whether past values of canary metric $X$ improve prediction of downstream metric $Y$ beyond $Y$'s own history; Granger precedence establishes temporal predictive improvement, not true causality~\cite{shojaie2022granger}.
We apply 5{,}000 permutations~\citep{phipson2010permutation} on first-differenced series with Benjamini--Hochberg FDR correction at $q{=}0.05$ across 8 validated canary$\to$downstream pairs (2 canaries $\times$ 4 downstream metrics).
Three properties distinguish PermG: a nonparametric null distribution robust to the short non-stationary series typical of iterative training~\cite{boettiger2012limits}, built-in directionality (forward and reverse tested separately), and a hyperparameter-free test statistic.
The remaining four methods each exhibit a specific limitation: naive cross-correlation has 75\% null-control FPR; differenced cross-correlation detects bidirectionally without directional separation; threshold onset is power-limited at $T{=}11$ under corrected $3\sigma$ calibration (0/8 significant in 8 of 12 cross-architecture conditions); Toda--Yamamoto~\cite{toda1995statistical} achieves moderate supplementary detection (3--4/8 at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$) with reduced power from degree-of-freedom costs of lag augmentation.
Per-method dose-response profiles, Shapley value analysis, and the full MMCT algorithm appear in the Appendix.

\subsection{Signal-Times-Resolution Framework}
\label{sec:theory}

We apply standard statistical power scaling to PermG under the Signal$\times$Resolution (S$\times$R) framework.
Detectability of canary$\to$downstream temporal precedence depends on two competing factors:
\begin{equation}
    \text{Detectability}(\alpha) \;\propto\; S(\alpha) \times R(\alpha),
    \label{eq:detectability}
\end{equation}
where $S(\alpha)$ is signal strength (magnitude of distributional shift, monotonically increasing with $\alpha$) and $R(\alpha)$ is temporal resolution (the generational gap between canary and downstream responses).
$R(\alpha)$ is non-monotonic: at low $\alpha$, entropy and diversity respond in different generations ($R$ large); at $\alpha{\approx}0.60$, relaxation time matching compresses both responses into a single generation ($R \to 0$); at high $\alpha$, the severity of entropy collapse outpaces the diversity cascade, restoring the generational offset.
The product $S \times R$ predicts four regimes: \emph{blind} ($\alpha \leq 0.45$; $S$ below detection floor), \emph{onset} ($\alpha \approx 0.50$; $S$ crosses threshold while $R$ remains high), \emph{synchronous dip} ($\alpha \approx 0.60$; $R \to 0$ suppresses detection despite rising $S$), and \emph{detection} ($\alpha \geq 0.75$; $S$ dominates).
Full empirical confirmation appears in \S\ref{sec:regime} and \S\ref{sec:dose_response}.
